ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all ISC holders, directors, officers, authorized signatories and principal franchise counterparties against: (i) the consolidated Canadian sanctions list administered by Global Affairs Canada under the Special Economic Measures Act, United Nations Act, and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Magnitsky sanctions); (ii) the OFAC SDN List and OFAC sectoral lists for any USD-denominated cross-border royalty wire; (iii) the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List; and (iv) public records of criminal convictions and Interpol Red Notices. PEP/HIO determination is mandatory under PCMLTFA and FINTRAC guidance, with Enhanced Due Diligence required for foreign politically exposed persons, heads of international organizations, and constituent legal persons; the franchise's payment rails (Franchise_Royalty_Wire and Local_POS) are classified Low_Risk_Standard, requiring ongoing transaction monitoring, suspicious transaction reporting to FINTRAC under section 7 of PCMLTFA, and periodic re-screening at least annually or upon material ownership change.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.ubo_and_aml_profiling_notes: The Ontario ISC register is not a public register; access is limited to authorized government authorities, law enforcement, and tax authorities. All UBO disclosures must be updated within 15 days of any change in significant control.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Ontario Business Registry (OBIS - Ontario Business Information System), administered by ServiceOntario under the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery; mandatory NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) report obtained through a licensed search house prior to corporate filing
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names under the Ontario Business Corporations Act must be expressed in English and/or French using Latin-alphabet characters only; a bilingual name is acceptable but each language usage must be distinctive and non-confusing. Non-Latin scripts (e.g., Chinese characters for the boba tea brand) must be transliterated into English or French for the legal corporate name; registered trademarks may retain original script but the corporate name cannot. Only limited punctuation and symbols are permitted (e.g., % & . - ' #); names must not be deceptively misdescriptive of the business, geographic origin, or corporate status.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name rejection by the Director of the Companies and Personal Property Security Branch, the applicant may: (i) revise the proposed distinctive and descriptive elements and re-file using the same NUANS report within its 90-day validity window; (ii) submit a written reconsideration request to the Director setting out statutory grounds under OBCA section 9 and supporting trademark and NUANS search evidence; (iii) if reconsideration fails, apply to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice under OBCA section 12 for an order directing the Director to permit the name, or incorporate as a numbered company and subsequently pass articles of amendment to adopt an approved name; (iv) acquire a fresh NUANS report and re-initiate reservation. No separate public administrative appeal tribunal exists; the practical window for correction without new fees is within the 90-day reservation period.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible with conditionality: OBCA section 14 requires a registered office in Ontario at a physical, staffed location accessible during business hours; a commercial virtual-office suite or corporate-agent premises is accepted only if a real location exists and records receipt and forwarding services are operative. A mail-drop or post-office box is not acceptable. For this franchise head-office profile, the Canada Revenue Agency and municipal food-premises regulators require actual operational substance; therefore the registered office may be a shared-service suite, but a physical Ontario operations location for the boba syrup supply chain, inventory, payroll, and IP administration must exist for tax and licensing validity.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Quantified annual risk: (i) unannounced municipal public-health inspection of retail and franchise boba premises under O. Reg 493/17 (Food Premises Regulation) is approximately 80-90% in the first operating year; (ii) CRA GST/HST or corporate income tax field-audit visit to the registered office is approximately 10-12% per year given substantial cross-border royalty and supply-chain flows; (iii) unannounced verification of the corporate registered office by the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery is under 2% per year. Aggregate risk classification: registered-office spot-check risk is Low; franchise-premise health inspection risk is High.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC), federal tax administration portal: My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/my-cra-business-account) and Business Registration Online (https://www.canada.ca/en/services/taxes/business-taxes/business-registration-online.html). Ontario corporate income tax and HST are administered by the CRA under the federal-provincial tax collection agreement; the Ontario Ministry of Finance (https://www.ontario.ca/page/tax-information-administration) remains competent for Ontario specific tax programs (e.g., Employer Health Tax, Ontario Innovation Tax Credit).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Incorporate or register extra-provincially under the Canada Business Corporations Act (via Corporations Canada, online at ised-isde.canada.ca) or under the Ontario Business Corporations Act (via the Ontario Business Registry online); both are recognized as CA_CORP (Inc./Corp.) with limited liability. Step 2: Obtain a 9-digit Business Number (BN) from the CRA through Business Registration Online (BRO), by filing Form RC1 Request for a Business Number, or by contacting the CRA Business Registration telephone service; the BN is the single statutory tax identifier used by the CRA and the Ontario Ministry of Finance. Step 3: Select program accounts when applying: RT (corporate income tax), RT (GST/HST), RP (payroll), RM (customs/import-export), each identified by a 7-digit program account suffix (e.g., BN 123456789 RT0001). Step 4: For a non-resident franchisor without Canadian incorporation, complete Form RC1 and attach foreign incorporation documents and proof of a Canadian permanent establishment or a Canadian agent; the CRA will assign a BN and the applicable program accounts if the entity carries on business in Canada or is required to collect GST/HST. Step 5: Register the Ontario nexus with the Ontario Ministry of Finance; no separate Ontario tax ID is issued because the BN is the common identifier, but Ontario-specific registrations are required if the business holds alcoholic beverages, tobacco, or other regulated goods (relevant for boba tea food and beverage operations). Step 6: Enrol for CRA online access (My Business Account or Represent a Client) within one business day after BN issuance; electronic filing of the T2 corporate income tax return and the GST/HST return is mandatory for all registrants with annual taxable supplies over CAD 1.5 million; smaller entities may file electronically or by paper but must still remit through financial institution or CRA online. For a federal corporation with a physical presence in Ontario, typical BN and program account issuance occurs within 1 to 5 business days for online applications.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation: A Canadian-resident Business Corporation (federal or Ontario) is a separate person and taxpayer under Part I of the Income Tax Act (ITA); pass-through treatment is not available for corporations regardless of shareholder count or ownership. Resident status is statutorily deemed for any corporation incorporated in Canada after April 26, 1965 (ITA s.250(4)); therefore CA_CORP is a Canadian resident corporation subject to full worldwide taxation. Federal corporate tax and Ontario corporate tax apply (Ontario tax is collected by the CRA); the corporation will ordinarily qualify as a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) unless it is controlled by one or more non-residents or by public corporations, which makes it eligible for the small business deduction on first CAD 500,000 of active business income (subject to clawback rules for associated corporations and adjusted aggregate investment income). Territorial scope: worldwide income taxation for resident corporations with a foreign tax credit system; controlled foreign affiliate rules (ITA s.91-95) apply only where the Canadian corporation holds 10% or more equity in a foreign affiliate. Tax exemption zones: none apply in Ontario, except for specific enumerated statutory exemptions (e.g., municipal or federal crown entities), which are irrelevant to a boba tea franchise.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no US-style check-the-box election; entity classification for federal and Ontario tax purposes is governed by the ITA and the CBCA/OBCA. Available statutory elections and mechanisms include: (1) ITA s.85 rollover election to transfer eligible property into the corporation on a tax-deferred basis; (2) ITA s.256(9) and s.156/156.1 elections to allocate the aggregate CCPC business limit among associated corporations; (3) ITA s.115/216 elections for non-residents to elect net-basis taxation on certain Canadian-source rental, timber, or mining income (not typically relevant to franchise royalties, which are subject to Part XIII withholding on outbound payments); (4) Excise Tax Act (ETA) s.156 joint election to treat supplies between GST/HST registrants who are related or closely related as made for no consideration, enabling cash-flow simplification in the corporate group; (5) ETA s.227.2 Quick Method election for small GST/HST registrants with worldwide taxable supplies not exceeding CAD 400,000; (6) ETA s.212 streamlined accounting for charities (not applicable); (7) hybrid mismatch recharacterization rules under ITA s.94B and s.94C, which may disallow deductions or include amounts in income where cross-border payments give rise to double-deduction, deduction/non-inclusion, or tax-transparent mismatches with a non-resident affiliate; (8) Excessive Interest and Financing Expenses Limitation (EIFEL) rules under ITA s.18.2/18.21 and 18.23 for taxation years beginning on or after October 1, 2023, which restrict net interest and financing expenses exceeding CAD 250,000 to a fixed ratio of tax EBITDA (a group-level election may alter the allocation of the group ratio); (9) elections under ITA s.159/220(2.1) for late-filed and amended elections where the CRA general anti-avoidance or waiver provisions apply. All elections must be filed with the CRA within prescribed statutory deadlines (typically three years after the filing-due date of the relevant return) to be valid.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) — a federal value-added tax administered by the CRA. Ontario is a participating province; since July 1, 2010, Ontario applies HST at 13% (5% federal GST component plus 8% Ontario provincial component). The GST/HST is a credit-method VAT: registrants collect tax on taxable supplies made in Canada, claim input tax credits (ITCs) for GST/HST paid on inputs, and file periodic returns (CRA Form GST/HST Return, generally monthly, quarterly, or annually depending on total annual taxable supplies).
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000: the small-supplier threshold is the amount of total consideration (before expenses) for all taxable supplies, including zero-rated exported supplies, made by the person and its associated persons in a single calendar quarter or in the aggregate of the four immediately preceding consecutive calendar quarters (other than supplies of financial services). Once the threshold is crossed during a calendar quarter, the person must register for GST/HST within 29 days of that day. A boba tea franchisor that exports syrups and supplies franchise services to non-resident franchisees is fully entitled to register voluntarily (or must register if the threshold is exceeded) so that it may claim ITCs on purchased goods and services; a non-registrant small supplier cannot claim ITCs. There is no separate Ontario provincial VAT registration; the BN and HST program account covers the combined 13% HST obligation.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No_Real_Time_Fiscal_Clearance_Mandate: Canada has not enacted mandatory real-time e-invoicing, digital stamping, API-based pre-clearance, or clearance of invoices by the CRA before issuance. A voluntary pan-Canadian e-invoicing standard based on the Peppol format is being implemented by the CRA through a certified access point (pilot phase began in 2024); the federal government continues to consult on possible mandatory B2B e-invoicing, but no legislation is in force as of the current fiscal period. GST/HST invoice content requirements are set out in ETA s.223: the supplier's name and BN, the recipient's name, the date, a description of the goods or services, the total consideration, and the amount of tax or a statement that the supply is zero-rated or exempt. Electronic invoices are acceptable if the information is reliable and accessible; receipts for supplies under CAD 30 are exempt from the full invoice-content rules. There is no requirement to obtain a digital stamp or prior clearance from Ontario or the CRA, but all invoices, export declarations, bills of lading, and payment receipts must be retained for six years for audit purposes.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating (0% GST/HST) applies to: (a) exports of goods (e.g., boba tea syrups, tea powders, packaging, and equipment) where the supplier ships the goods directly out of Canada or delivers them to a common carrier for export in accordance with ETA Schedule VI Part V s.1; (b) services supplied to a non-resident recipient (e.g., franchise licensing, training services, marketing and supply-chain management services addressed to foreign franchisees) under ETA Schedule VI Part V s.7, provided the service is not in connection with real property situated in Canada or tangible personal property situated in Canada, and is not a service performed wholly to an individual present in Canada (non-resident corporate franchisees do not constitute individuals, so training to corporate employees performed abroad qualifies); (c) supplies of intangible personal property (franchise rights, trademarks, trade names, know-how, recipes) supplied to a non-resident who will not use the intangible property in Canada under ETA Schedule VI Part V s.10, which is the operative provision for royalty and franchise-fee revenue from foreign franchisees. For goods, the supplier must retain documentary proof that the goods were irrevocably removed from Canada, including the customs export declaration and a bill of lading; for services and intangible supplies, the supplier must obtain evidence of the non-resident status of the recipient (e.g., foreign incorporation certificate, foreign tax residence certificate, proof that the foreign franchisee has no permanent establishment in Canada). Zero-rated supplies are taxable supplies, so the registrant CBSA-retained exporter may claim full ITCs for GST/HST paid on inputs used to make those supplies; net GST/HST refunds are paid through the regular GST/HST return.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration — Canada Export Declaration (B13A/CAED) filed through the CBSA Canadian Export Reporting System (CESR/CARM); the declaration must show the exporter name and BN, the foreign consignee, the tariff classification, the quantity, the value, and the port of exit, and must be retained together with the CBSA 'proof of export' stamp or electronic confirmation

Bill of Lading — an ocean bill, air waybill, or truck/rail waybill naming the Canadian seller as shipper, the non-resident franchisee or buyer as consignee, and showing the port/place of departure in Canada and the destination outside Canada (with container and seal numbers where applicable); a sea or air waybill alone is accepted by the CRA as corroborative evidence, but must be accompanied by the export declaration for shipments above CAD 2,000

Inward Remittance Certificate (IRC) — a bank-issued IRC, SWIFT MT103 credit advice, or a bank statement showing receipt of the foreign-currency proceeds from the non-resident franchisee into the Canadian corporation's Canadian bank account; where intercompany settlement is applied, a signed intercompany settlement statement between the Canadian franchisor and the related foreign franchisee must be retained to evidence the receipt of consideration
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA and the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) conduct targeted audits of export zero-rating claims. If the exporter cannot produce the mandatory documentation bundle, or if the documentation is fabricated or inconsistent, the CRA may reassess within four years (indefinitely if misrepresentation is proven) to apply 13% HST on the supply deemed made in Ontario, deny ITCs, and charge compounded daily arrears interest. Civil penalties: ETA s.280(1) imposes a penalty of the greater of CAD 100 and 25% of the net tax sought to be evaded for false statements or omissions made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence; ITA s.163(2) imposes a gross-negligence penalty equal to 50% of the understated tax; a failure to obey a CRA compliance order attracts additional fines. Criminal liability: ETA s.327 and ITA s.239 provide for fines of up to 200% of the evaded tax and imprisonment for up to five years for wilful tax evasion, including false export claims and fictitious foreign remittances. Directors and officers may be jointly liable for amounts held in a deemed trust if the corporation fails to remit. Mitigation measures: retain the export documentation bundle and all underlying records for at least six years (ETA s.286); obtain annual non-resident status certificates from each foreign franchisee; document the transfer-pricing methodology for franchise royalties and syrup pricing in accordance with ITA s.247 to avoid penalty-level adjustments; and ensure that foreign-currency consideration is repatriated to Canada within 180 days of the supply date, as the CRA regularly applies the 180-day intercompany benchmark and ITA s.17 may deem interest income on outstanding non-resident trade receivables for services that are not settled within that period.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) is the issuing and central monetary authority; OSFI supervises all federally chartered Canadian banks; FINTRAC enforces AML/CTF reporting. Canada has no separate foreign-exchange administration or currency-control commission; foreign-exchange policy is implemented through an open, floating-rate framework.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible. Both current-account items (franchise royalties, management fees, trade payables, and supply-import disbursements) and capital-account items (shareholder equity injections, intercompany loans, dividends, and capital repatriation) may flow freely across borders without exchange-control licensing or central-bank approval. Profit remittance is subject to ordinary corporate law, sanctions screening, FINTRAC wire-reporting thresholds, and Canadian non-resident withholding tax under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act where dividends, rents, royalties, or interest are paid to non-residents.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory surrender, repatriation window, or mandatory conversion ratio for export or royalty receipts. A bubble-tea franchise treasury may retain USD, CNY, or other currencies in approved accounts or convert to CAD as commercial need dictates. Records must nevertheless substantiate the commercial substance of every transaction for GST/HST, corporate income tax, customs valuation, and FINTRAC monitoring.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility: Medium for payment-orchestration and low-value remittance; Low for primary treasury settlement. Under the Bank Act, only a chartered bank or an authorized deposit-taking institution may accept deposits in Canada; offshore digital EMIs therefore cannot lawfully open a Canadian deposit account. Such platforms may operate only as licensed or registered payment service providers under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) and provide payment functions without banking privileges. A franchise treasury should use a Schedule I or Schedule II bank as the principal clearing bank; fintech EMIs may be used solely for store-level payout automation, franchisee reimbursements, and e-wallet fronting where the underlying funds are not treated as deposits and no derivative credit risk is taken.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Canada permits both physical and remote corporate identity verification. In practice, tier-1 banks require at least one authorized Canadian-resident director or officer with signing authority to complete an in-branch identity interview unless the bank has implemented an approved video-identification channel. Fully remote opening is not universally available for corporations with non-resident ownership or franchise license intellectual property elements. For the highest clearance certainty, the President or CFO should attend a physical interview with original corporate documents, while non-resident directors may satisfy identity requirements through notarized passports, proof of address, and a corporate resolution naming the Canadian resident signatory.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Ultimate beneficial ownership is obscured by a multi-tier holding structure, including parent entities in Hong Kong or Delaware.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Diagrammatic ultimate-beneficial-ownership schedule showing every individual holding at least 25%, Ontario Business Registry profile, certificate of incorporation and constating documents, consolidated organizational chart, board resolutions, and formal source-of-funds declarations for all opening contributions.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large recurring cross-border payments for syrups, tapioca pearls, and packaging from suppliers in China, Taiwan, Vietnam, or Thailand.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed master supply agreements, pro-forma invoices, packing lists, bills of lading or airway bills, customs entry records, Incoterms 2020 statements, supplier licensing/KYC packs, and a rolling inventory-to-payable forecast evidencing commercial reasonableness.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Franchise royalty collections create explosive revenue growth that cannot be reconciled with point-of-sale transaction data.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Franchise disclosure documents, executed franchise agreements, audited financial statements, CRA notices of assessment, monthly POS and merchant-account statements, royalty calculation summaries, store-opening schedule, and unit-level sales reconciliations supporting the 4-8% gross-sales royalty assumption.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Disproportionate cash-intensive retail operations and rapid bank-deposit velocity across multiple tea shops.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Daily cash-drop logs, Interac/Visa/Mastercard settlement records, GST/HST and PST sales filings, internal cash-management policies, bank deposit receipts, and surveillance-ready store sales reports.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Payments to jurisdictions perceived as money-laundering or sanctions risks (e.g., certain Asia-Pacific counterparties, shell financial centres).
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Detailed counterparty compliance files, commercial contract evidence, valid end-beneficiary ownership structure, export/cargo tracking, and enhanced due-diligence questionnaires, plus OFAC, UN, EU, and Canadian sanctions screening results.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital injections should be routed through direct SWIFT MT103 or Fedwire-equivalent correspondent clearing into the Canadian bank concentration account. The remittance field should specify 'Shareholder equity contribution' or 'Intercompany shareholder loan' with the Ontario corporation's name and bank account identifiers. Canadian banks require the originator bank to perform standard due diligence, and the receiving bank will verify the corporate resolution and beneficial-ownership filing before the funds are made available. No exchange-control formality applies, but the corporation should maintain a capital-call resolution, subscription agreement, share certificate register, and source-of-funds evidence to credential the board record and any future financing.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade and treasury disbursements use layered clearing rails: (1) high-value cross-border royalty and supply payments use SWIFT MT103 via banks participating in SWIFT gpi with ISO 20022 remittance; (2) large equipment purchases from foreign factories use irrevocable commercial documentary letters of credit (L/C at sight), with transport documents and inspection certificates as required; (3) Canadian-dollar vendor and franchisee settlements use Payments Canada Lynx for high-value same-day clearing and the ACSS for low-value pre-authorized debits; (4) USD payments clear through CHIPS or Fedwire correspondent balances; (5) store-level franchise royalty collections are aggregated through Interac Direct Payment, Visa/Mastercard POS acquiring, and merchant settlement sweeps into the central treasury.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable CAD/USD, CAD/EUR, CAD/CNY, CAD/JPY forward contracts executed under an ISDA 1992/2002 Master Agreement with CSA support, typically tenor 1-24 months.
FX swaps for liquidity matching between CAD operational inflows and USD/CNY supply-chain outflows.
Cross-currency interest-rate swaps to convert long-term franchise-expansion debt into CAD or USD liabilities as prescribed by ALCO policy.
Plain-vanilla foreign-exchange options and zero-premium collars written by tier-1 bank dealing desks for budget-rate protection on procurement and royalty repatriation.
Exchange-traded Canadian-dollar futures and options listed at the Montréal Exchange and cleared through the Canadian Derivatives Clearing Corporation for exchange-traded hedge recognition.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) referencing non-fully-deliverable Asian currencies (for example INR, IDR, PHP, TWD) are permissible OTC hedges where the underlying procurement settlement is nominated in a restricted or thinly traded currency and subject to OSFI margin requirements and internal derivative-risk limits.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Ontario Annual Return (OBCA s. 113(1) for Ontario-incorporated corporations; Corporations Information Act for extra-provincial corporations registered in Ontario)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Director, Companies and Personal Property Security Branch, ServiceOntario, Ontario Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after each anniversary of incorporation (or anniversary of extra-provincial registration in Ontario for a federally incorporated franchise entity)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No graduated late fee is published; failure to file for two consecutive years permits the Director to administratively dissolve the corporation under OBCA s. 241. Revival requires Articles of Revival, all outstanding annual returns, and prescribed revival fees.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA s. 263.1) - required only if the franchise entity is incorporated federally and holds an Ontario extra-provincial licence
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after each anniversary of CBCA incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file for two consecutive years may result in dissolution by the Director under CBCA s. 212 after notice of default; revival requires an application, payment of overdue annual-return arrears, and prescribed revival fees.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal corporate income tax and Ontario corporate tax filed jointly via the T2 with Ontario schedules)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); Ontario corporate tax is administered federally through the T2 filing
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due no later than 6 months after the corporation's fiscal year-end (e.g., June 30 for a December 31 year-end)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: ITA s. 162(1) late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per complete month of delay up to a 12-month maximum; repeat failure (ITA s. 162(2)) yields a 10% penalty; CRA-prescribed daily compound interest applies to outstanding balances; gross negligence may trigger penalties under ITA s. 163(2).

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual ISC/UBO Register Verification - Register of Individuals with Significant Control (OBCA s. 140.1)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Maintained at the registered office; available for inspection by the Ontario Director, law enforcement, and other prescribed authorities under the OBCA (no annual filing to a registry is currently required in Ontario)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Ongoing duty; update the register within 15 days of learning of a change in significant control; reconcile annually alongside the Ontario Annual Return anniversary cycle
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to maintain or correct the ISC register is an offence; directors or officers may be liable on conviction to a fine of up to CAD 5,000 and/or imprisonment for up to six months; continuing default may also be cited in administrative dissolution proceedings.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual GST/HST Return (franchise royalty remittances, syrup supply sales, and licensing revenue) - if the registrant is on an annual filing cycle
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For annual filers, due within 3 months after fiscal year-end (annual filing is generally available where worldwide taxable supplies are CAD 1.5 million or less; monthly and quarterly filers follow the CRA-assigned remittance schedule)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: ETA s. 280 penalty of 5% of unpaid net tax plus 1% per complete month of delay up to 12 months; CRA-prescribed daily interest; repeated failures can trigger security requirements, asset seizure, or prosecution.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No monetary threshold triggers a mandatory audit. An OBCA non-distributing (private) corporation avoids an audit only while all shareholders unanimously pass an annual resolution dispensing with the auditor (OBCA s. 148). If any shareholder withholds consent, or if the corporation is a distributing corporation, an independent auditor must be appointed. The CRA may also compel financial statement audits on a discretionary risk basis; full accounting records and royalty ledgers must remain available.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: CPA Canada Handbook: IFRS for publicly accountable enterprises; ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) is permitted for private Ontario corporations. Franchise royalty revenue and syrup supply transactions are recognized under IFRS 15 (five-step revenue model) or ASPE Section 3400, as elected. Financial statements must be prepared to support the T2 even when no audited statements are statutorily required.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Ontario's OBCA s. 140.1 requires every non-exempt corporation to maintain a Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC/UBO) at its registered office. An ISC is any individual who directly or indirectly owns or controls 25% or more of voting shares, holds 25% or more of voting rights, or exercises de facto control. The corporation must verify UBO data annually, record share transfers in the Register of Members, and update the ISC register within 15 days of knowledge of any change. For a cross-border boba tea franchise, the global franchisor must maintain a traceable chain of significant control and ownership for the Canadian entity.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book (including by-laws, shareholder and director minutes, and resolutions)
Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC/UBO)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 220-450 (CAD 300-600) per annum for a Toronto or Ontario registered office plus corporate secretarial and annual-return filing service
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 2,200-7,400 (CAD 3,000-10,000) for a full statutory audit of a small franchise business; USD 1,100-2,600 (CAD 1,500-3,500) for an annual review engagement if the OBCA auditor waiver is renewed by unanimous shareholder consent
